note: Few foreign records charted in the US in the 1940s; foreign list kept short.

Billboard's national best-seller chart only starts 27 Jul 1940; earlier-1940 placings come from Wikipedia's year ranking in '1940 in music'. No race or hillbilly chart existed: the two country rows rest on a retrospective ranking in '1940 in country music'; no r&b, gospel, latin or polka hit could be tied to 1940 by a source. 'Frenesi' (2 weeks at #1 in Dec 1940, 11 in 1941) is filed under 1941. No foreign-act hit sourced.

Pop rows from the full-year Billboard best-seller chart. No race chart yet (Harlem Hit Parade starts Oct 1942), so no r&b row; country rows use the hillbilly positions quoted in '1941 in music'. Xavier Cugat is US-based, counted home. No foreign-act hit sourced.

Full pop evidence. The recording ban began 1 Aug 1942 but stockpiled masters kept the year's chart full. Harlem Hit Parade only starts 24 Oct 1942 (one r&b row); the country row rests on the retrospective ranking in '1942 in country music'. No foreign-act hit sourced.

AFM recording ban (Aug 1942-Nov 1944; Decca and Capitol settled autumn 1943, Victor and Columbia Nov 1944) thins this year: hits were stockpiled pre-ban masters, reissues ('All or Nothing at All', recorded 1939) and a cappella vocal records (the Song Spinners). Country rows: hillbilly positions from '1943 in music'/'1943 in country music' (no Billboard folk chart until 1944). Xavier Cugat counted home. No foreign-act hit sourced.

AFM recording ban (Aug 1942-Nov 1944; Decca and Capitol settled autumn 1943, Victor and Columbia Nov 1944) thins this year: Decca (Crosby, Andrews Sisters, Mills Brothers, Ink Spots, Louis Jordan) and Capitol (King Cole Trio) had settled and dominate; Columbia's Harry James hit is a 1941 master. Country from the new Most Played Juke Box Folk Records chart (Jan 1944). 'Don't Fence Me In' (peak Dec 1944-Jan 1945) is filed here. No foreign-act hit sourced.
Full evidence across pop, race and folk charts. Gospel row: Sister Rosetta Tharpe peaked #2 on the race chart (May 1945). No foreign-act hit sourced.
Billboard year-end (retail sales) plus race and folk jukebox number ones. No gospel, latin or foreign-act hit tied to 1946 by a source.

Billboard year-end (retail sales) plus race and folk jukebox number ones. Ray Noble (British, US-based since the 1930s, with American singer Buddy Clark) counted home. 'Heartaches' is a 1930s Ted Weems recording revived in 1947. 'Ballerina' peaked across late 1947/early 1948, filed here. No foreign-act hit sourced.

Billboard year-end (retail sales) plus race and folk number ones. Second recording ban (all of 1948) pushed a cappella/overseas-recorded and pre-ban masters. Foreign: two British records on the year-end list. Gospel row is weak: the source gives Mahalia Jackson's December 1947 release and sell-out sales but no chart year.

Billboard year-end top 30 (retail sales) plus R&B and country number ones. 'Mule Train' (Frankie Laine, year-end #9, peaking into 1950) and 'Baby, It's Cold Outside' left out for space. No gospel, latin or foreign-act hit tied to 1949 by a source.
